migrationNotes: Spine: one plank on two posts with a crate. Saw it in two to find the shear, then the bending moment, then see how a spread load and a single load shape the moment, and finish by following the moment along the plank to find where it peaks.
Left out of the lesson (still in the course): engr-shear-and-moment-8, a multiple-choice item on the sign of a shear force; the first try and the shear screen cover it.

lesson.title: Shear force and bending moment

lead.text: Suppose you saw the plank in two, 2 m from the left end, and somehow keep both pieces exactly where they were. Before the cut the left piece was at rest, and it stays at rest, so the forces on it must still balance. The left post pushes up on it with 9 kN. The crate is further along, on the other piece. Nothing else pushes down on the left piece, so the cut face must supply a 9 kN downward force.
That force across the cut is the shear force, written V. Its size equals the sum of the vertical forces on the left piece, and we count upward forces as positive, so here V = +9 kN.

You could keep the right piece instead. The 15 kN crate pulls it down and the 6 kN post pushes it up, which leaves 9 kN downward that the cut face must hold up. The answer has the same size, and it acts the other way, as the two faces of a cut should.
Cut the plank, keep the left piece, and ask what must act on it for it to stay at rest.

steps.headline: How the shear changes along the plank

lead.text: Slide the cut along the 10 m plank and the shear force follows it. For any cut between the left end and the crate, the left piece holds only the left post's 9 kN, so V is +9 kN along that whole stretch. Move the cut past the crate and the 15 kN crate joins the left piece, pulling it down. Now V = 9 − 15 = −6 kN. The picture plots the shear along the plank.

afterFigure.text: The shear jumps at the crate by the crate's own 15 kN and then stays at −6 kN to the right-hand end. The minus sign says that the net force on the left piece now points downward, and its size, 6 kN, matches the right post's push. That has to be so, because that post alone is left to hold up the right-hand piece.

lead.text: The load sits at x = 2 m. Cut just to the right of it, so that the left reaction and the load are both on the left piece.

Shear is only half of what a cut face does. The left piece has a post pushing up at one end and a cut at the other, and a push at a distance twists a piece, as a spanner twists a nut. For the piece not to turn, the cut face must also supply a turning effect. That is the bending moment, written M. It is the total moment of all the forces on the piece, taken about the cut.

On the 10 m plank, cut under the crate, 4 m from the left end. The left piece has one force on it, the post's 9 kN, acting 4 m from the cut, so M = 9 × 4 = 36 kN·m. A cut 2 m from the left end gives 9 × 2 = 18 kN·m. A moment that bends a beam into a smile, hollow side up, is called sagging and counts as positive. The forces on the right piece give the same moment, so use whichever piece has fewer forces.
A moment is a force times its distance from the point you take moments about.

steps.headline: A 6 m beam on end supports carries 15 kN at x = 4 m. Find the bending moment under the load.

lead.text: Here is the whole method, line by line.

workedSteps.text: Find the left reaction with moments about B.
Cut under the load. Only RA is to its left, 4 m away.

steps.headline: On the 6 m beam, the 12 kN crate is at x = 2 m and the left reaction is 8 kN. Find the bending moment under the crate.

lead.text: The method is the same as in the worked example.

workedSteps.text: Cut just under the crate. Only the left reaction is on the left piece.
It acts 2 m from the cut. Multiply, in kN·m.

steps.headline: A load spread along the beam

lead.text: Not every load sits at a point. A floor or a layer of snow spreads its weight along the beam, and engineers give it in kilonewtons per metre, kN/m. A uniform load of w kN/m over a span of L metres weighs w × L in all. For finding moments it can be treated as that single weight, acting at the middle of the stretch it covers. The picture shows a beam carrying 2 kN/m over 6 m, and the same weight gathered at midspan.

afterFigure.text: That load weighs 2 × 6 = 12 kN, so each post holds up 6 kN. Cut at midspan, 3 m from the left end. The left piece has the post's 6 kN pushing up 3 m from the cut. It also carries half of the spread load, 2 × 3 = 6 kN, pulling down with its centre 1.5 m from the cut. So M = 6 × 3 − 6 × 1.5 = 18 − 9 = 9 kN·m.

Done in symbols for any uniform load, the same steps give M = wL² ÷ 8, which here is 2 × 36 ÷ 8 = 9 kN·m. By symmetry, midspan is where this beam is bent most. Gathering the same weight at midspan, the second case in the picture, bends it more, because none of the weight is spread towards the posts.

lead.text: The largest moment is at midspan. Use the result from the last screen, or balance the left half of the beam yourself.

steps.headline: A single load, and a cantilever

lead.text: A single load gives a simpler answer. Put a load P at the middle of a beam of span L. By symmetry each post carries P ÷ 2. Cut under the load and the left piece has P ÷ 2 acting L ÷ 2 from the cut, so M = P ÷ 2 × L ÷ 2 = PL ÷ 4. For a 6 m beam with a 12 kN load at midspan that is 12 × 6 ÷ 4 = 18 kN·m.

A cantilever is a beam held by a wall at one end and free at the other. Cut it next to the wall and look at the free piece, which has only the load acting on it. The moment is then the load times its distance from the wall, so a 4 m cantilever with 6 kN at its tip has M = 6 × 4 = 24 kN·m at the wall. It bends the other way from a plank, hollow side down. That is called hogging, and a hogging moment counts as negative.

steps.headline: Shear is the slope of the moment

lead.text: Go along the 10 m plank from the left end and watch the moment. It starts at zero, because no force lies to the left of a cut at the very end. Each metre you move the cut to the right adds the shear to the moment, so the moment rises by 9 kN·m per metre while the shear is +9 kN. That is the general rule: the slope of the moment curve at any point equals the shear force there. The picture shows the moment and the shear of the plank side by side.

afterFigure.text: After the crate the shear is −6 kN, so the moment falls by 6 kN·m per metre. It comes down from 36 kN·m at the crate to zero at the right-hand end, as it must at a post with nothing beyond it. The moment curve is highest where it stops climbing and begins to fall.

lead.text: Look at the top of the moment curve on the last screen, and use the slope rule on what is happening there.

lesson.orientation: Cut a beam, balance one piece and draw how shear and moment vary along it.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A plank 10 m long rests on a post at each end. A crate of 15 kN sits on it, 4 m from the left end. From the earlier lessons you know what the posts do. The left post pushes up with 9 kN and the right post with 6 kN, and the plank stays put because those two pushes balance the crate.

That tells you what happens at the ends and nothing about what goes on inside the wood. At every point along the plank one side is pulling or pushing on the other, and some places work much harder than others. A plank that snaps does so at one particular place, and an engineer needs to know which.

This lesson saws the plank in two, in the imagination, and asks what the cut face must do to keep each piece where it was. That gives two quantities at every point along a beam, one for sliding and one for turning. Together they show where the beam is most at risk.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the shear force and bending moment at any cut along a beam, and say where the moment peaks.

recap.keyIdea: At any cut, the shear force is the sum of the vertical forces on one piece and the bending moment is their total moment about the cut. The moment peaks where the shear passes through zero.

blocks.text: Back at the plank, the cut at 2 m carried a shear of 9 kN, and the cut under the crate carried a moment of 36 kN·m, the largest anywhere on it. On the shorter beam you found a shear of −4 kN just beyond a 12 kN load and 16 kN·m under it. A uniform 3 kN/m over 8 m peaks at 24 kN·m, at midspan, where the shear passes through zero.

recap.nextHook: The bending moment squeezes one face of a beam and stretches the other. The next lesson works out how hard the material is working at those faces.

questions.prompt: A 6 m plank rests on a post at each end, with a 12 kN crate 2 m from the left end. The left post pushes up with 8 kN. Cut the plank 1 m from the left end. What force, in kN, must the cut face supply to keep the left piece still?
hints: The left piece is still, so the forces on it must balance.
What pushes up on it, and is anything pushing down?
The crate is not on this piece.
questions.onCorrect: 8 kN. Each piece must still balance after the cut, so the cut face supplies the force: the shear force.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole crate, which sits to the right of the cut and is not on the left piece.
That is the right post's push, which acts on the far piece.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only the post's 8 kN acts on the left piece, so the cut face must supply 8 kN the other way.

questions.prompt: The left reaction is 10 kN upward and nothing else acts on the left piece. What is the shear force at the cut?
hints: Count upward forces on the left piece as positive.
questions.onCorrect: Upward forces on the left piece count positive, so the shear is +10 kN.

misconceptions.feedback: An upward force on the left piece counts positive, so the sign is the other way.
The reaction is on the left piece and nothing cancels it, so the shear is not zero.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: +10 kN. The only force is 10 kN upward, so V = +10 kN.

questions.prompt: A 6 m beam on end supports carries 12 kN at x = 2 m, so the reactions are 8 kN at A and 4 kN at B. Find the shear force just to the right of the load, in kN, counting upward forces on the left piece as positive.
hints: Add the vertical forces on the piece to the left of the cut.
Just right of the load, both the reaction at A and the load are on the left piece.
Calculate 8 − 12, keeping the sign.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Left of the cut: +8 kN reaction and −12 kN load, so V = 8 − 12 = −4 kN.

questions.onCorrect: −4 kN. The downward load outweighs the reaction, so the shear changes sign across it.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the sign: the load is downward, so just to its right the shear is negative.
That is the shear just left of the load. Just to its right the load is on the left piece too.

questions.prompt: A 5 kN upward force acts on the left piece, 2 m from the cut. Find its moment about the cut in kN·m.
hints: A moment is force times perpendicular distance.
The force is 5 kN and the distance is 2 m.
Multiply them.
questions.onCorrect: 10 kN·m. The bending moment adds up force times distance for every force on the piece.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the force and the distance. A moment multiplies them.
That divides the force by the distance. A moment multiplies them.

questions.prompt: Why is it enough to use only the forces to the left of the cut?
hints: What must be true of both pieces once the beam is cut?
questions.onCorrect: Both pieces are in equilibrium, so one side's forces are enough. Pick the side with fewer forces.

misconceptions.feedback: Forces on the right do have moments about the cut. They simply give the same answer as the ones on the left.
Neither side is stronger. The beam is the same either way.

choices.label: Each piece balances on its own, so either one gives the same moment.
Forces to the right never produce a moment.
The left side of a beam is always the stronger side.

acceptedIdeas: Each piece balances on its own, so either one gives the same moment.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each piece balances on its own, so either one gives the same moment.. Each piece is in equilibrium, so one side's forces give the whole moment.

hints: Only the left reaction is on the left piece.
Multiply that force by its distance from the cut.
Calculate 8 × 2.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only RA acts left of the cut: M = 8 × 2 = 16 kN·m, sagging.

questions.onCorrect: 16 kN·m: the left reaction times its distance. The crate itself acts at the cut, so it adds no moment.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the reaction, not a moment. Multiply it by its distance from the cut.
That uses the crate's weight, but the crate acts at the cut and adds no moment.

questions.prompt: An 8 m beam on end supports carries a uniform 3 kN/m along its full length. Find the largest bending moment, in kN·m.
hints: By symmetry the peak is at midspan.
Use wL²/8, or balance the left half about the cut.
Calculate 3 × 8² ÷ 8.
questions.onCorrect: 24 kN·m at midspan: wL²/8, or the left half balanced about the cut.

misconceptions.feedback: That is wL² without dividing by eight.
That is each reaction, a force. The peak moment multiplies forces by distances.

questions.prompt: Along a simply supported beam, what is the shear force where the bending moment reaches its peak? Answer in one word.
hints: The slope of the moment diagram equals the shear force.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Zero: the moment's slope is the shear, and the slope vanishes at the peak.

questions.onCorrect: At the top of the moment curve the slope is level, so the shear there is nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: At the top of a hump the curve is neither rising nor falling. Shear is its slope, so ask which value means a level slope.

questions.prompt: A 3 m cantilever carries 5 kN at its free end. Find the size of the bending moment at the wall, in kN·m.
hints: Cut at the wall and look at the free piece.
Only the end load acts on it.
Calculate 5 × 3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The load acts 3 m from the wall: M = 5 × 3 = 15 kN·m, hogging.

questions.onCorrect: 15 kN·m: the free piece has one force, so the moment is that force times its distance.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the force. Multiply it by its distance from the wall.
That adds force and distance. A moment multiplies them.

questions.prompt: A 10 m beam on end supports carries 20 kN at midspan. Find the largest bending moment, in kN·m.
hints: Find the reactions by symmetry.
The peak is under the load.
Calculate 10 × 5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each reaction is 10 kN; under the load M = 10 × 5 = 50 kN·m. This is PL/4.

questions.onCorrect: 50 kN·m under the load: one reaction times its 5 m distance, which is PL/4.

misconceptions.feedback: That is each reaction. Multiply by its distance from the load to get a moment.
That multiplies the reaction by the whole span. The distance to the cut is half of it.

questions.prompt: An 8 m beam on end supports carries 24 kN at x = 6 m, so the reactions are 6 kN at A and 18 kN at B. Find the shear force just to the right of the load, in kN, counting upward forces on the left piece as positive.
hints: Add the vertical forces on the piece to the left of the cut.
Both the reaction at A and the load are on that piece.
Calculate 6 − 24, keeping the sign.
questions.onCorrect: −18 kN. The load outweighs the reaction at A, and the shear equals minus the reaction at B.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the sign: just right of a downward load, upward forces on the left piece are outweighed.
That is the shear just left of the load. Just to its right the load is on the left piece too.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Left of the cut: +6 kN reaction and −24 kN load, so V = 6 − 24 = −18 kN, which matches B's reaction.
